summary_html: CPS **screens out** a report (no investigation) or closes as **unfounded** after minimal review. Federal law (CAPTA) conditions funding on operating screening criteria and recordkeeping; federal reviews (CFSR) assess decision quality.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — screening & intake system requirements  
- **CFSR Regulations (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal performance/quality review of state screening and responses

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Beattie v. Aiken County Department of Social Services
key_cases.holding: The court held that parents whose case was closed as unfounded may not examine the DSS case file, that 'report' covers all investigative information and the reporter's identity is never disclosable, and that FOIA requires separation and release of non-exempt material where a court is asked to conduct that review.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling authority on what happens to records after a screen-out or unfounded determination — they are sealed and slated for destruction.
key_cases.quote: The clear language of § 20-7-650 prohibits the disclosure of the DSS case file to Appellants or to anyone else.

key_cases.case_name: Kaci May v. Dorchester School District Two
key_cases.citation: Op. No. 6053 (S.C. Ct. App. filed May 29, 2024) (App. Case No. 2020-001352)
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals of South Carolina
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of an injunction, holding S.C. Code § 63-7-920(C) authorizes DSS to interview children at school without a warrant and outside the parents' presence during a mandated investigation, and that the interviews here were reasonable in inception and scope under the Fourth Amendment.
key_cases.relevance: The court notes the statutory duty to determine whether a report is 'indicated' or 'unfounded' and the discretion the agency holds in doing so.
key_cases.quote: we find § 63-7-920(C) expressly authorizes DSS to interview children at school without a warrant when conducting an investigation mandated by § 63-7-920(A)(1)

key_cases.case_name: South Carolina Department of Social Services v. Wilson
key_cases.holding: The court held that a parent facing an intervention petition and entry on the Central Registry has a protected liberty interest and a due process right of confrontation, and that allowing the child to testify outside his presence without an individualized finding of trauma violated that right.
key_cases.relevance: It marks the line between closing a case and seeking intervention, which is the decision point a screen-out or unfounded closure sits on.
key_cases.quote: Because Wilson did not have the opportunity to be heard in a meaningful manner, his due process right was violated.

key_cases.case_name: Jensen ex rel. Estate of Clark v. Anderson County Department of Social Services
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals, adopting the six-element special duty exception to the public duty rule and holding that the Child Protection Act imposes on the local child protection agency and its social workers a special duty to investigate and intervene whose breach may give rise to a private cause of action, with immunity turning on remand on whether the duty breached was ministerial or discretionary.
key_cases.relevance: Closing a report as 'unfounded' is protected only if a thorough investigation preceded it; Jensen treats the duty to investigate thoroughly as ministerial, so closing a file for want of facts forfeits official immunity.
key_cases.quote: the Act imposes a special duty on the local child protection agency and its social workers to investigate and intervene in cases where child abuse has been reported

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit reversed, holding that the confidential retention of records of a child abuse investigation classified 'unsubstantiated' and 'ruled out' violates neither substantive nor procedural due process, so the state officials were entitled to qualified immunity.
key_cases.relevance: Hodge holds that a family cleared at intake has no federal right to have the 'unsubstantiated' record destroyed, which is the federal backdrop against which Beattie's state confidentiality and destruction rules operate.
key_cases.quote: The record before us presents no substantive due process violation of a familial privacy liberty interest by virtue of the retention of the Hodge investigation report
